big: The Rao family has ₹8 crore spread over 17 funds and four goals that nobody has written down. Their problem is rarely returns. It is the missing structure, and that is where a good adviser starts.

lines: My husband has funds, I have funds, and my father-in-law's old ones are still there. Where do we even start?
With goals and dates, not funds. Then we ask to see everything together, because only then can we tell what each fund is for.

alt: A cost counter rising with inflation while equity share steps down into safer funds over eight years
caps: A masters abroad costs ₹1.2 crore today. Assume costs rise 8% a year.
The price climbs each year. With eight years to go, the money starts mostly in equity.
As the date nears, equity steps down into safer funds, so a fall cannot wreck the plan.
By year 8 the bill is about ₹2.22 crore, and most of the money has moved to safe funds.

alt: Four bars showing the debt, equity and gold mix for a three-year, eight-year, twenty-year and thirty-year goal
caps: Same family, four goals. Each has its own date, so each gets its own mix. Assumed, for illustration.
A home deposit due in 3 years sits mostly in debt. A fall must not reach it.
Education at 8 years takes a middle mix. Retirement at 20 years carries more equity.
Legacy money may stay untouched for decades, so it can hold the most equity.
The date sets the mix first. Fund choice comes after.

intro: What a whole-family review of the Raos' funds finds (made up).
note: Mapped to goals, perhaps six funds would do, each with a named job. The client gains a simple plan, fewer repeat bets and one view of tax.

q: A client with about ₹8 crore across 17 funds and some fixed deposits asks you to "suggest something good". What is your best opening move?
opts: Show him the fund with the best 3-year return on your list
Ask for his goals, then review all holdings together
Offer a new NFO, since HNIs like being early in new ideas
Tell him to sell the weakest five funds and buy a flexi-cap
why: Pitching a product before any goal repeats the habit that gave him 17 funds. Past return says nothing about his plan.
Goals and dates tell you what each rupee is for, and a full view shows what he already holds. Recommendations come after.
Being early is no virtue without a goal it serves. An NFO has no record, and he already holds many funds.
Selling the weakest five funds judges by return alone, and may trigger tax. You cannot judge a fund before you know its job.

q: A client has ₹5 crore in one flexi-cap pot. She needs ₹2 crore for a home in 30 months and plans to retire in 18 years. What is the sound first step?
opts: Split the money by goal, and move the home money to low-risk funds
Keep it all in flexi-cap, since equity beats debt over the long term
Put everything into debt, since part of it is needed soon
Switch to gold, since neither goal has a fixed amount
why: Each goal has its own date. Money due in 30 months cannot depend on equity, while the 18-year money can stay invested.
Equity may win over decades, but the home money is needed in 30 months, when a fall could leave a gap that cannot be refilled.
Part of the money has a long horizon. Putting all of it in debt would starve the retirement goal of growth.
Gold can be part of a mix, but it carries its own swings. Neither goal is solved by one asset, whatever its amount.

q: A masters abroad costs ₹1.2 crore today. Costs rise 8% a year, and the daughter leaves in 8 years. What target should the plan use?
why: This ignores eight years of rising costs. Plan for today's price and the plan will fall short by the time she leaves.
This adds 8% of the base eight times, as if simple interest. Costs compound, because each year's rise applies to a higher price.
₹1.2 crore grown at 8% a year for 8 years gives 1.2 times 1.08 to the power 8, about ₹2.22 crore.
That is the cost after only 4 years of rises, half the time. The daughter leaves in 8 years, not 4.

q: An HNI client's 12 funds hold large gains, and consolidating at once would create a big tax bill. What do you propose?
opts: Hold all 12 for good, since a tax bill is never worth paying
Stop new money into duplicates and phase exits over tax years
Redeem everything in March and rebuy at once for a clean start
Ignore the tax, because a simpler portfolio matters more than cost
why: Tax is a cost to weigh, not a reason to keep duplicates for good. The running cost of 12 overlapping funds also adds up.
New money goes to the keepers at once, and staged exits spread gains over years. Agree the plan with his CA first.
One-day exits push all gains into one tax year and may trigger exit loads. A clean start is not worth that bill.
Tax is real money, and for an HNI it is large. A simpler portfolio is the aim, but cost and tax shape how you get there.

pts: Start from goals and dates, then map each goal to a horizon, a mix and only then a fund.
HNIs care about tax, liquidity, succession and one clear view of everything they own.
Ask to review all holdings together. A simpler plan is the gain for the client, and it earns the trust.
